subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May 7, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bennett.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house is the annual and historic motion that the house do now go into committee of ways and means to consider provisions as to the ways and means for the forthcoming year. On this particular occasion the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is asking the house to supply over $400,000,000 for expenditure during the coming year. Throughout the whole of his statement he failed to give one syllable or a single intimation of how he proposes to raise this vast sum of money. True, in a general way we know the sources from which it will come, but it has been customary, and indeed the main theme of a budget is to indicate to the house precisely how the government expects to raise the money for which they ask. This particular feature the minister has wholly ignored. There is however before parliament a demand for $400,000,000, and he gives to the house what purports to be a budget speech in which he indicates very extensive changes in the tariff, but he does not indicate whether there will be an increase or a lowering of revenue, or what effect these changes will have upon the taxation and revenue of the country. He simply says to this house and to the country, Figure it out for yourselves. We 
have a right to ask, and we purpose asking the minister, to indicate to the house in a very full and detailed manner the effect of these changes.
Apart from this major oversight on the part of the minister there are three main features to the budget speech-imperial preference, countervailing duties and the growth of foreign trade. I think these may be claimed to be the chief points of the budget speech and I intend briefly to examine them. I shall deal first with imperial preference.
I am sorry that neither the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) nor the Minister of Finance is in his seat. In years gone by I think it has been the custom for the Minister of Finance to remain in his seat-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and listen to any criticism which may be offered so that he may give the proper consideration to such criticism. I can remember one occasion in the year 1922 when the late Mr. Fielding, who sat throughout the budget debate, changed his budget and brought in a second one as a result of the debate and suggestions from this side of the house. The present Minister of Finance however not only utterly fails to give to the house any suggestion as to how he purposes to raise the $400,000,000 but he will not even sit in the house and listen to the discussion of the meagre budget for which he is responsible. I might 'point out further that he was not in his place yesterday; in fact there were only one or two ministers in their seats yesterday.

speechtext:
country to grant to the overseas dominions some preferences in those markets. The time has come when we should make it perfectly clear to the mother country that if this imperial preference is to continue it must be a two-way preference.
Now I will briefly run over what the various dominions already have done, and I am going to give only the rough percentages because to go into detail would be wearisome. These are the rough percentages of what the overseas dominions have accorded to the mother country in the way of preferences: Australia, 10 per cent and in some cases as high as 20 per cent; New Zealand, 10 per cent to 20 per cent; Irish Free State, one third of the duty on motor cars, 30 per cent to 50 per cent on imported wines and a reduction of one sixth of the general tariff; Rhodesia, 10 per cent to 12 per cent; Union of South Africa, generally speaking about 5 per cent; on motor cycles and electrical appliances, 15 per cent; India allows a preference of 17 per cent on iron and steel goods. Then there is a long list of small dependencies and colonies where the preference runs from 5 per cent to 20 per cent. In Canada the general advantage to Great Britain, as compared with the general tariff, is 10 per cent to 12 per cent, without taking into account the changes of to-day.
There are other features in connection with the imperial preference which might well be studied by parliament and by the government. These are privileges which have been extended to us by the mother country, and we might very well consider if there are any such privileges which we could extend to them. The Trustee Securities Act of 1893 provided that securities for trust funds, including stocks of empire concerns, would be included in the classes of trustees' securities, in this way facilitating the borrowing of money in the old country. Then there is the Empire Marketing Board, to which the British government grants $5,000,000 a year. This is an excellent gesture and serves a very good purpose. There is the Merchandise Marks Act of 1926, which calls for the marking of goods with the place of origin. There is also the Films Act of 1927, calling for an increase in the proportion of films made by British companies or by companies within the British Empire, and we must remember also that government purchases are restricted to United Kingdom and empire goods. At the recent Imperial conference the McKenna duties of 1915 on motor cars, musical instruments, gloves, watches, films, cocoa, coffee, dried and preserved fruits, sugar, tobacco and so on were revived, and in

1925 Mr. Churchill also gave certain other preferences on sparkling and ordinary wines and other articles. I will not go into full details.

speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
expect that the mother country will give a preference to Canadian agricultural products such as wheat and so on against the Argentine?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will answer that question in a moment; I am coming to that very point now. Now I want briefly to run over a few items in which Canada is very much interested and with regard to which I think we have reason to ask for some preferential treatment in the British market. I want to make it clearly understood that I am not suggesting for one moment that the list which I shall give is comprehensive at all.
Let us consider minerals, for instance; take copper first. Great Britain imports about
160,000	tons of pure, refined copper per year; she is one of the largest importers of copper in the world. Of that amount only 14,000 tons comes from within the empire; the balance comes from the United States, Spain and other places. I think we have a perfect right and I believe it would be a sound principle to say to the mother country, " Here, we are a big producer of copper; we desire to supply some of your requirements." Most of our copper for the past thirty years has gone to the United States; 82 per cent of our production goes to that country in the form of ores or in concentrates, not even smelted, and in addition a large quantity is in blister copper which goes to that country for refin-The city of Tacoma on the Pacific coast, in the state of Washington, has virtually as its chief industry a big smelter which depends entirely on the ores from Howe Sound, just north of Vancouver. Daily thousands of tons of concentrates go past our doors at Vancouver to maintain this huge industry in the city of Tacoma. I have not the figures for the last year or two, but some time ago I went into this question with great care and found that 82 per cent of the copper produced in Canada went to the United States in the form of ores or concentrates. They smelted, refined and merchandised those ores, and where did they sell them? Of the purchases made by Great Britain, 64 per cent came from the United States, consisting largely or in part at least of the copper which we produced, and from which we only got the cost of digging it out of the ground. In that respect I say we have a right to tell the mother country, " Here is an article upon which we can come to some understanding," and I

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
believe the result would be that the Britisher could get his copper cheaper and we could get more for it, because in the merchandising of copper or any other article, that is in the trading between merchants, there is a profit as well as in the smelting and refining.
Then let us consider lead, of which 40 per cent of Great Britain's requirements come from other than the empire. Great Britain is a big importer of lead. Consider the question of silver, and just here let me say a word or two about silver. I could take an hour to discuss this question but I am just going to say this: I believe at the. next Imperial conference Canada particularly- because we are vitally interested-ought to bring to the attention of the empire the great question of silver, silver coinage and the remonetizing of silver. I am not going into the intricate and complex question of the remonetizing of silver, but its history is a tragedy. There is no doubt of this in my mind. In 1873 one billion people in the orient, in China, in India, in the Malay states and in Mexico, were deprived of two-thirds of their purchasing power by the action of the nations of that day. That is one reason for the agricultural and commercial depression which exists to-day all over the world. One half of the human race is living below the margin of decent living. In fact, millions upon millions in China, during this present year, have died largely because of the inadequacy of their purchasing power. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, this matter of silver is the biggest subject before the people of the world today. I call attention to it merely because we are a big producer of silver. Great Britain is a large importer, having imported during 1927 55,000,000 ounces of silver. During the same period, India imported 116,000,000 ounces, and nothing would help Canada, Mexico and the United States so much as the solution of this complex silver problem.
Great Britain in 1927, imported 150,000 tons of zinc, principally from Belgium, Germany and the United States. To-day our zinc is selling, I think, for 3 cents a pound.
A moment ago I pointed out that in 1819 Great Britain gave this country a preference in the British market for timber, and that was the basis of the great timber business carried on in Ontario and Quebec. I can recall from my earliest days in Canada-there are others who can go back much farther-seeing rafts of timber going down the St. Lawrence river to the historic city of Quebec, which was at that time the centre of the timber trade of Upper and Lower Canada. What are the facts to-day? Great Britain imports 550,000,000
cubic feet of lumber-I am not giving the board measure, but it can be obtained by multiplying by 12-of which 521,000,000 cubic feet, or 94 per cent, comes from sources other than the British Empire. Canada should be able to secure a larger share of this market. We were told by the British economic commission which sat a year or two ago, presided over, I believe, by Lord Lovat, that at the present rate of consumption the soft woods of the world would be exhausted within 30 years. I cannot say whether or not that estimate is correct, but that statement is contained in the official report. We all know that our great forests are being denuded at an alarming rate. Canada has great forests, and there should be a reasonable conservation of these great resources, but we are entitled to a greater share of the British market. During the past two or three years the exporting of lumber from Canada has been an unprofitable business because it has been necessary to carry it on as close to the margin of profit as is possible. I was told by one of the largest exporters in Canada that although to-day he is exporting three times the amount of lumber that he did some two or three years ago, he has made a smaller profit. This small margin of profit is caused by competition from Russia, Finland, the Baltic states, and so forth.
I now take up the question asked a moment ago by my hon. friend-that of wheat. Slightly more than one-half of the wheat products imported into the United Kingdom during 1927, were imported from foreign sources. I will repeat in part what I said before the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) took his seat, that I have no hesitancy in saying to the mother country that if this great doctrine of imperial preference and interimperial trade is to prevail, if it is to mean anything, it must be reciprocal. There must be two parties to the bargain. That is one of the things which must be asked of the mother country, not with the idea of taxing food but rather of a preference to be granted on Canadian wheat. The question may be asked: how are we going to do that except by taxing food? I will grant that, but it also involves a complete change in the fiscal policy of the mother country. It is not our business to tell the mother country what her fiscal policy should be, but it is our business to tell her that if this empire is to be sustained, econonimic laws, as well as sentiment, must apply. They will have to sit around the table with us and determine what preference we are going to have in their markets. The mother
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

country has been purchasing the subsidized wheat of Germany, and the overplus of France; she has been combing the world for wheat.
I am not here to apologize for or defend the Canadian pool, because I know very little about its internal workings. There is a very acute problem facing Canada in so far as the marketing of her wheat is concerned. Responsibility rests upon the shoulders of the government to face a national problem of this kind. I will tell the Prime Minister that it will not do to say that that is the business of the cooperative societies handling these things. There comes a time when private enterprise cannot function in the face of great national difficulties, and that time has arrived in connection with wheat. One of the solutions for this problem is the securing of a permanent and larger share of the British market.
I do not propose to go any farther into this imperial preference except to say that the extension of this preference should be mutual and should be based upon an intelligent appreciation of the internal interests of both parties; otherwise it can be only mischievous.

speechtext: How can we obtain that English market for our wheat?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have no desire to repeat myself, but I told my hon. friend a moment ago that it is not our business to dictate to the British authorities what they shall do. Surely two intelligent groups could sit down together and decide these things. One advantage which they want is access to our markets; this government is pretending to give them that access. In turn for that, we have the right to say: Give us a preferential access to your market for some of our vital products.
V hen the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was emphasizing the other day the need of looking after Canadian interests, the Prime Minister interjected the remark: What of the empire? I ask the Prime Minister:	What of the empire for the last five
years? The figures which I will now give show that this condition has been chronic for the last thirty years, and has been accelerating during the last six or eight years. The average figures for the last five years show that we imported $746,000,000 worth of goods from the United States and exported $482,000,000. During the year 1930 the imports amounted to $847,000,000 and the exports $514,000,000. The average figures for five years for the United Kingdom show imports of only $180,000,000 and exports of $411,000,000. Let us look these figures squarely in the face. This thing has been going on for some thirty years. Why
FMr. Stevens.]
the anxiety just now? Is it simply because there is surcharging the atmosphere the suggestion of interimperial trade? Why is it that the Prime Minister has not in any one of the seven years since 1923 when he was a party to passing that resolution at the Imperial conference, acted, although he said at the time that the matter was urgent. Why is it that in the year 1930, just before an election, it now becomes important? Why is it he says t.o my honoured leader: What about the empire to-day? What about the empire last year, or the year before, or the year before that?
Let us examine further this imperial policy and budget. In nearly 50 per cent of the items I find there has not been any change whatever. Why, the Minister of Finance stood in his place the other day and assumed an air of tragic importance when he said: This involves changing some 500 items in the tariff. He endeavoured to impress upon us the magnitude of the change and that was headlined throughout the country. This was to be a great general revision of the tariff. I counted the items and I think there are 420 instead of 500, but of those there are at least 178 in regard to which there is not an atom of change in duty, the only change being that they are arranged in a different order. In eighty-five others affecting the British preference the change is so slight that it will never be noticed. Let me give one instance:
Malt flour containing less than 50 per centum in weight of malt.
And so forth. This is to be a great concession to the British producer of malt, but the change is one-tenth of one per cent down. In other words, if you paid $10 in duty before the budget was passed, you would pay $9.90 after it was passed, and there are eighty-five articles very little better than that, so that we whittle the matter down to a pretty narrow compass. That is not all. There are other changes which are merely annoying without being of any advantage to the mother country. Let me give an illustration. We have built up in Canada a very fine electrical appliance manufacturing business to manufacture electric lights, switches, wiring and so forth. In Ontario, for instance, there are several large industries built up on that basis. There has been a reduction in the duty on the items: Electric light fixtures and appliances.
Electric head, side and tail light; electric torches or flashlights.
Electric arc lamps and incandescent electric lamps.
And so forth. I cite these merely as an illustration. The change is from 20 to 15 per

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
cent and it is simply a trifling, annoying change. It is a question whether anybody will derive any advantage except that it may open the market a little so as to lessen the purchases from Canadian firms and, I venture to say, without changing one iota the price to the consumer. If the government were going to put these things on the free list; if they were going to transfer the business to Great Britain as, under their scheme of inter-imperial trade, they pretend they are going to do, why did they not put them on the free list and put these firms out of their misery? On the other hand, if they have some consideration for Canadian industry, why do they not allow a reasonable, protective tariff to remain on an industry that has been up over a period of thirty-five years? I remember well thirty-five or thirty-six years ago when the first sod was turned in the city of Peterborough for the Canadian General Electric, that huge firm which has gradually grown up and established one of the greatest industries of the country. It is concerns like this that are giving our people a livelihood, an opportunity to make their way in Canada. Why jeopardize them? Why annoy them? If the government are going to have a policy which will put industry out of business, let them say so. If, on the other hand, we are going to have a policy that will give Canadian manufacturers a chance at the Canadian market, then let us retain the duties as they are.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that. I have my own views on these matters and I am presenting them. If my hon. friend knows of any manufacturers who are pleased with the changes, let him bring them along; the government will be glad to receive them.
Let me say a word or two in regard to countervailing duties. This is a feeble response to a nation-wide wave of indignation against this United States economic penetration. Will the Prime Minister do me the honour of recalling an occasion just about five years ago when we were concluding the budget debate of that session, when I said to him words to this effect, that if his policies were persisted in, the inevitable result would be the economic absorption of Canada by the United States? I think I was laughed at on that occasion, but yesterday we had it from the lips of one of his bright young followers that the reason for what we have before us now is that the United States has, during recent years, so penetrated Canada in an unfair competition that the government has at last been driven to take this action. The Prime Minister and his government come before parliament and in effect say this: We are conscious that throughout Canada there is a wave of indignation against the economic penetration of Canada by the United States under most unfair conditions. So they say: We have imposed countervailing duties. That is the government's answer. Let us examine these countervailing duties. They cover some eighteen items out of some twelve or fifteen hundred in the tariff. That is no answer. It will answer only if it is not discussed, only if the Prime Minister can get over to the public the idea of a countervailing duty against the United States without going into the details and an exposition of just what the application is. It is no answer at all; it is simply the answer of a small boy looking around the corner at the town bully and sticking his tongue out at him. If this thing is serious, if these countervailing duties are to become
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

the doctrine and policy of Canada, apply them to the tariff as a whole. Apply them on a broad basis.
Let us look at some of these eighteen articles to which the countervailing duties are to be applied. First, animals. I suppose that these duties will apply to goats, sheep, baby chicks and a few things like that. They also apply to live hogs, canned meats and other meats, tallow, beeswax, eggs. I will admit this, that with respect to eggs, so long as the United States duty is eight cents a dozen, a countervailing duty will be partly effective, but should Uncle Sam just in a playful mood decide to lower his duty to four cents, the protection would be gone overnight.
Take fruit and vegetables. On fruit and vegetables the countervailing duties will apply during the winter months when they are not very much required, but when the period of glut comes when the orchards of Wenatchee are able to unload their surplus fruit on a salvage basis, or when there is a glut of vegetables coming in from the southern states at the time when our own fresh vegetables are coming on the market, at that time your countervailing duties will not be worth a snap of your finger. The government repealed the only protection we had against that sort of thing, namely, the dumping clause, and they have refused to listen to the appeals for a seasonal tariff. This answer of the government, Mr. Speaker, is not an answer. These countervailing duties will not do the job. Furthermore, limited as they are to eighteen articles, it is the mere gesture of a schoolboy as compared with what it should be, and that is a frank notice to the United States that we are not going to tolerate longer the condition that exists in this regard.
I must hasten on. I wish to refer briefly to foreign trade. This has been heralded by hon. gentlemen opposite, and particularly by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson), who said yesterday:
Canada has made greater progress in foreign trade than any other country in the world.
He also declared in the same speech that he wanted British export trade to prosper. That is all right. I want British export trade to prosper in the interests of Britain. But I want Canadian trade also to prosper. I want my hon. friend, who is a student and intelligent, to follow me in a very brief argument if I can get time to put it across to him.
He will admit this, that the United Kingdom has an excess of imports and is a loaning country. I do not think those two facts will be disputed. Her imports are paid for in three ways:	(1) By exports; (2) by services,
such as shipping and so forth; and (3) by 
interest on investments. Canada, on the other hand, is a borrowing country, having borrowed six billions of dollars or more upon which she must pay interest abroad every year, which at five per cent amounts to $300,000,000 annually. So Canada is under the necessity of exporting $300,000,000 worth of goods to pay for that item alone. Canada imported last year $1,265,000,000, and she has to pay for that with exports, adopting the free trade doctrine that exports pay for imports. In addition, Canada has little carrying business of her own; she pays British and foreign shipping for her carrying. She will pay out annually about $150,000,000 in carrying charges, and she must pay for that with exports. So you have the sum of $1,715,000,000 that she must pay for with exports, and her exports amount to $1,388,000,000, leaving a deficit of $327,000,000. How do we cover that deficit? By borrowing abroad and gradually mortgaging the Dominion more and more year by year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always pleasant to listen to a speech such as was delivered by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Stevens). One cannot but admire his fine flow of language, and to some extent one can almost follow his logic. It seems regrettable that one of the ablest debaters on the opposition side should have announced his retirement from public life, but even yqt let us hope that the report of his retirement, like the report of Mark Twain's death, is greatly exaggerated. I shall not attempt to follow his argument in detail. Rather I shall direct myself to the general policy of criticism that was enunciated the other day by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) himself.
The leader of the opposition was somewhat at sea with regard to a definition of the budget. As we all know, each year the government meets and listens to the representations made by the various members representing the constituencies throughout Canada. We all know how diversified the interests of our country are, and after listening to all these representations the government brings down a policy which sums up and crystallizes into legislation the general needs of the people of Canada as a whole. I think in this respect the government has done exceptionally well in the budget. In fact, I do not think ever before has any budget met with such general unanimity of endorsement as the budget that has just been presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). It would be foolish to say that all members on this side of the house agree with the budget in every detail.

The Budget-Mr. Hepburn
One could not expect that. One could not expect the leader of the opposition to bring down a budget which would meet in detail with the approval of every member of his party. I would like to ask, for instance, how he would reconcile the conflicting interests of his friends from the maritimes, who are seeking a higher rate of duty on coal, with the interests of the Conservatives from British Columbia who would be very glad to see a reduction in the duty on coal. So we have to look at the matter in its broad aspects.
I think that this budget has so confused the leader of the opposition that after his three hour speech on Tuesday he had demonstrated only two things-one that he was completely in the woods and had not yet seen his way out, and the other that it had apparently developed in him a sort of vindictive spirit which probably prompted him to introduce his motion of want of confidence in the words he used, charging the government with insincerity and with having lost the confidence of the country.
I do not know any member who should hesitate more to charge the government with insincerity than the hon. leader of the opposition himself. What was his stand on the liquor export bill? He said that during the session of 1926, when the Conservatives were in power, or thought that they were in power, they adopted a motion to the effect that liquor clearances should be stopped, and so he says, " I am the father of this political child." Then he went on and dramatically rose to great heights, waggling his finger across the floor at the Liberals and censuring them for not having brought down the legislation before, and he said that it was because Liberals were participating in what he called a "rat fund." The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) pointed out that in the report of that same commission, a gentleman from Vancouver-I shall call him a gentleman- admitted that he was the financial agent for the Conservative party, and that he had accepted funds for that party from that source. That took the wind completely out of the sails of the hon. leader of the opposition. His speech on that occasion only went to show that he could use a great volume of words, use a machine gun to slay a mosquito and could make a mountain out of a mole hill. He stated in reply that he had not read the whole report of the commission which he tried to use for the purpose of criticising the Liberal party. Now, as parliamentarians, we must accept the word of the hon. gentleman, but I venture to say that when he came to the
part which told of his party participating in the campaign funds from the liquor interests he must have stuck his tongue in his cheek and closed one eye. Not only has he claimed parentage to the liquor clearance bill, but he also states that all the good children in the budget belong to him, and all the bad ones to the Liberal party. Further, he claimed paternity of the proposed imperial conference. I think the hon. gentleman is so politically prolific that instead of being known as the leader of the Conservative party he might well be called George Washington, the father of all good ideas in our country.
He assailed some hon. gentlemen on the front benches of the Liberal party rather vigorously, particularly the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Crerar). Well, I do not think he detracted very much from the high esteem in which those gentlemen are held by the people of Canada. He went further, he also attacked the present chairman of the tariff board, Mr. Moore. He attacked him because of the fact that Mr. Moore was at one time connected with the Mackenzie and Mann interests. Evidently attacking men formerly with these people is an obsession on the part of the hon. gentleman; for I remember that at one time he attacked even Mr. Meighen and dubbed him the megaphone of the Mackenzie and Mann interests, although afterwards he was content to be a loyal follower of Mr. Meighen. While he was bringing under his condemnation former associates of the Mackenzie and Mann interests, I thought he might very well have gone down the front ranks of his own party. Had he done so he would have found that the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae) was-so I am informed-a leading agent for the same interests, a gentleman who now guards the war chest of the Conservative party. If he did not profit by his connection with the Mackenzie and Mann interests, I think it was only his own fault. He surely missed an opportunity.
The hon. gentleman seems to think that disintegration is taking place on the government side. He might have applied to himself Burns' couplet:
O wad some power the giftie gie us,
To see oursels as others see us!
I cast my eye across the floor and observe the hon. member for Vancouver Burrard (Mr. Clark), one of the senior members of the Conservative party, who has announced his retirement from the party; as has also the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys), one of the ablest debaters on the opposition benches; there is also the hon. gentleman who



The Budget-Mr. Hepburn
has just taken his seat (Mr. Stevens), a former Minister of Customs in a Conservative administration. Glancing down the front opposition bench, I see missing the genial member from British Columbia, Doctor Tolmie, who even after he left the house had a disagreement with the leader of the Conservative party. Another hon. gentleman missing from the front benches opposite is Sir Henry Drayton, who is now gracing the liquor control board of Ontario as its chairman. There may be some extenuating circumstances in that respect, because anyone found drunk in Ontario might claim a certain degree of respectability from the fact of having purchased his liquor from an organization headed by a belted knight drawing a salary of $25,000 a year. Further down the front benches opposite we have two former Laurier Liberals, who certainly when they speak of the insincerity and deception of the Liberal party should be able to express themselves very feelingly on the subject. I am wondering what attitude my hon. friend the genial doctor from Fort William (Mr. Manion) will take following the introduction of this budget. Will he get up as he did last year, and dramatically with blood in his eye, talk about red-blooded Cana-dianism and be ready to stay here all summer hoping to take the Yankees out into the front yard and spank them?

speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Hepburn
Hon. gentlemen across the way say that there is nothing in the British preference; that it means nothing; that this new avenue of trade we are trying to open up is not capable of development. We know differently. I am not going to take. the time to read any of the comments of the British press, but I may [DOT]summarize by saying that the British press recognizes that this is not only a gesture of good will but a method by which the British industrialists can open up new avenues of trade for their produce and marketable goods and can in turn take care of the ever-increasing food production in Canada. We heard a great laugh from our Conservative friends when mention was made of placing fruits and vegetables upon the free list under the British preference. The laugh was on the other side of their faces however when the Minister of Finance announced that trade arrangements with the West Indies would permit the importation of a great quantity of fruits and vegetables. I listened intently and with great respect to the remarks of the leader of the opposition when he attempted to minimize the importance of our present trade arrangement with the West Indies. In this connection I wish to place on Hansard a statement issued by Mr. M. J. Hunter, president of the Toronto Fruit Protective Association:
When domestic fruits and vegetables are out of season it will tend to increase business with the West Indies. Until last year the Indies have not kept pace with the times in the marketing of fruit. They shipped it in containers such as their ancestors used seventy-five or one hundred years ago. Often the growers brought it down to the wharfs three or four days before the date of sailing. Then it was loaded on ships which had no refrigerator systems. They knew nothing about packing lettuce in ice, for example, as the California growers do. All the new Canadian National steamships have refrigerating systems to carry fruit, and representatives of the West Indian growers spent last year in Canada studying marketing methods and requirements.
He said iu conclusion:
At the same time any increase in the amount of fruit and vegetables brought in from the West Indies will not be a detriment to Canadian producers since they will only come in during the season when Canadian-grown fresh fruits are off the market.
On top of that we have a statement which appeared in The Ottawa Citizen a short time ago to the effect that a boatload of vegetables had arrived at the port of Montreal from Bermuda. It was announced that the whole cargo was sold out and many Ottawa merchants went to Montreal for the purpose of inspecting it. That would seem to be an indication as to the possibility of developing trade with the West Indies with respect to fruit and

vegetables. The fortunate part of it is that these fruits and vegetables can be imported from the West Indies during the season when Canadian-grown produce is off the market, and in return we can sell many of our marketable products to them. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition made some statement in regard to economics. His remarks may have been prompted by political motives, but I wish to say that I am always interested in getting the opinions of the leading economists. I have in my hand the opinion of two outstanding economists, one a Britisher and the other a Canadian. I shall refer first to the statement of Sir Benjamin Morgan, who was for ten years chairman of the British Empire producers, organization and is now vice-chairman of the Empire Economic Union:
These proposals will stimulate as nothing else could the desire throughout Britain to reciprocate by increased purchases of Canadian goods and will help to crystallize a policy that will make for the consolidation of the empire into one economic unit.
He goes on to state:
It is a great example to the empire and if we could embody the Canadian proposals in a commercial agreement with the mother country together with maximum reciprocities on the part of Great Britain, we should stabilize for a number of years the outlook for industries in both countries. Voluntary preferences in the past have suffered from being subject to revision or alteration in each succeeding budget, and the time has come when it would be to the advantage of the empire countries to replace voluntary preferences by a negotiated reciprocal commercial agreement. I hope this may be crystallized at the forthcoming imperial economic conference.
When an economist such as the one I have just quoted holds an opinion diametrically opposed to the opinion of the leader of the opposition, I am very much inclined to take the views of the economist, who points out that Canadians will find an increased market for their produce and at the same time the Canadian farmer will be guaranteed against the increased cost of production by this new trade which will develop with the British Empire.
I have before me the statement of another economist, Professor K. W. Taylor, the authority on public finance with the economics department of McMaster university. He is reported as having said among other things, the following:
Overseas trade has been built up by the government by the extension of the work of the Department of Trade and Commerce with the establishment of Canadian trade commissioners in foreign countries. The development of export trade must be done by the individual business man. All the banks and the government can do

The Budget-Mr. Hepburn
is to point the way. The reduction of tariffs to Great Britain will certainly build our overseas trade.
I was very glad to see that Mr. Dunning deprecated the tariff wars. The past 100 years has proved the futility of tariff wars.
In regard to British preference I wish to point out that while under our revised schedule some may say this is a high tariff budget, I would say on the contrary that it is very well balanced. If hon. members would study the schedule they would find that the rates have been greatly changed. In the general tariff 54 items have been increased and 46 have been decreased. Under the intermediate tariff 35 items have been increased and 98 have been decreased. Under the British preferential tariff the rate has been increased on 11 items and decreased on 270 items. When the revision is complete the tariff schedule will consist of 1,118 items, and of these 559 will be free under the British preference. I think it is futile and useless for our friends across the floor to argue that these changes will not stimulate trade and are not in keeping with the principle of trade extension advocated by the Liberal party.
I do not know just what is left for my hon. friends across the floor to talk about. It may be that they will bring forward the idea of the unfavourable trade balance, which seems to give them quite a handle as long as they can becloud the real truth of the matter. We must admit that this year we have an unfavourable visible trade balance of about $113,000,000, but we know very well, and any child should know, that if the marketable wheat had been sold out of this country we would have added about $225,000,000 to our sale of goods abroad, or perhaps more, and that shatters their argument with regard to the unfavourable trade balance. In the ordinary business of the year we are still ahead; in that respect I would say we have a favourable trade balance of about $112,000,000, and we have not taken into consideration the invisible trade balance of this country.
Coming as I do from the southern peninsula of Ontario I am in a good position to closely observe the American tourist traffic. It was estimated last year from reliable sources that our United States friends spent about $300,000,000 in this country in that period. Personally I believe that to be a conservative estimate; nevertheless we will accept it. That estimate was made by the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, by the Wall Street Journal and by various motor leagues throughout the country; and all these authorities go on to point out that it is possible for us in Canada to develop this business to a billion dollars annually. If we do that,
to a certain exent it will take away from our exportable surplus and, under the logic advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite, it will be possible further to confuse the people of Canada. However, I do not believe they will be able to confuse the people of southern Ontario, because those people know very well what is going on. In the summer time they see that about every other car on the highway is from the United States, and they realize that at least fifty per cent of the business done by the retail merchants of southern Ontario is carried on with American tourists.
It would be folly for this country to carry into effect the idea enunciated by my hon. friend who preceded me in this debate. He spoke of a general upheaval of the tariff. Supposing we carried out that policy in its entirety and increased the cost of all our goods in Canada. Then we would be in such a position that we could not offer these goods at attractive prices to our American friends. If the American government goes on increasing the tariff of that country, as it proposes to do, thus increasing the cost of all the articles the people of that country must buy, we will be able to offer them an extremely attractive proposition in the way of cheaper goods. I do not doubt that if we maintain this policy which is now before us, within the next five or six years ait least we shall be selling to tourists from the United States fully a billion dollars' worth of goods in our own country.
Then there is one other question, that of unemployment, to which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition made some reference. Well, the explanation of unemployment is very simple. We are living in a new era, an age of mechanization both of the farms and of the industries of Canada, and we realize that situation, which is very obvious to us when we see the displacemenlt of labour by machinery. As a farmer I see how this works out in carrying on my own business; I can do it with less labour than my grandfather needed. Now we have tractors; we have electrical equipment as well as all the other modern labour-saving devices on the farms, and we must buy and use these devices in order to be on a competitive basis. In the western provinces we have seen the introduction of the combine harvester, and we know the amount of labour being displaced in that way; we know that there may not be any more of the old time harvester excursions to the west. We see that sort of thing all along the line. We see the displacement of labour by machinery in industry as well. I am not going to attempt to place on Hansard any of the official figures in this regard, but

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the budget I am willing to admit that I do so with considerable trepidation. The subject is of such vast importance and can be approached from so many angles that one finds it difficult to decide just what questions to discuss.
Having been accustomed in the routine of daily life to devote my attention to the problems of health and disease, to seek the causes and effects of certain conditions that affect the health of my patients, I am forced to pursue a somewhat similar attitude in this debate. To-day I am to deal with a new patient-Canada-and try to ascertain whether or not the body politic is in a really healthy condition. Generally speaking, no one will deny that Canada has been enjoying a great measure of prosperity. The ship of state has been sailing on a kindly sea under very favourable trade winds, but of late certain conditions have arisen which portend a less favourable voyage. There are breakers ahead, and these breakers are to be found in our unfavourable trade balance for the past year, to the extent of some one hundred million dollars, in the general and widespread depression of business throughout the country, in the great amount of unemployment of our labouring classes, and in the slow and progressive atrophy of our basic industry, agriculture.
I have the honour, Mr. Speaker, to represent the good old county of Lanark, a county of vast and fertile acres, a county whose people are descendants of those early Scotch, Irish and English pioneers who inhabited the land

The Budget

Mr. Murphy
when it was a vast forest and hewed out homes for themselves under very trying conditions. This is a county that has endeavoured through years of toil and struggle to establish within its bounds important manufacturing industries, and last but not least a county which has given many of its sons and daughters to work for the general welfare of this great Dominion. I might remind you, sir, that our present capable and esteemed Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is a native son of that county.
At the outset I mentioned that Canada had been enjoying a fair degree of prosperity. I ask in all fairness, can that prosperity be due in any great degree to the policy of the present government? Can they take unto themselves credit for the bounteous crops with which Providence has blessed us? Can they assume the credit for having placed in that great precambrian shield those vast and untold mineral resources that are to-day undergoing such extensive development? Can they regard our great forest wealth as something of their production? And so I might proceed asking questions about the basis of our national wealth, and having done so I am
forced to the conclusion that none of these things can be accredited to any act of this government. Wherein, then, does the function of government apply, so that this great heritage which has been handed down to us may ibe developed for the benefit of us Canadians? In answering this question we must analyse the various policies of the government in so far as they may assist in promoting or retarding the development of our natural resources and our industries. It is my intention to deal first of all with agriculture.
Agriculture has been called our great basic industry. In fact, for a great many years it was the chief source of our national wealth. iHowever, during the past few years, and .especially since the great world war, it has failed to keep pace with the march of our industrial development. In studying these figures we can readily see that there has been a general decline in production not only in field crops but in animal products. In so far as field crops are concerned we cannot lay the blame on the government. Undoubtedly climatic conditions accounted mostly for the decline, and unfortunately for Canada and the farmer in particular the decline has been costly. The total value of field crops in 1927 was $1,173,133,600; in 1928, $1,125,003,000; in 1929, $979,750,400, or a decline of $193,383,200 in 1929 as compared with 1927. But it is in analyzing the figures of exports and imports, especially in animal products, that we find reason for alarm. Our exports of cheese have fallen in the four years from 134,000,000 pounds to 92,000,000 pounds and our imports have increased from 1,218,600 pounds to 2,103,700 pounds. Our exports of butter have fallen from 9,814,000 pounds to 1,400,400 pounds; and our imports have increased from 9,151,900 pounds to 35,928,200 pounds, a very alarming increase indeed. Surely something must have caused this tremendous slump in our great dairy industry, and upon investigation we find the cause to be the order in council by which New Zealand was permitted to export butter into Canada at one cent a pound duty. It has been argued that the people of Canada are eating more butter per capita. The figures on which this argument is based are mostly estimates, as there are no definite figures for dairy butter production. However, we know for a fact that in a great many counties there is also a marked decrease in the production of dairy butter. The bare fact remains that Canada, since the inception of the New Zealand order in council, has ceased to be a large exporter of butter, has not been able to supply her own requirements and has become an importing country. In view of this analysis, we must lay blame on the government. The present administration by that one act has adversely affected and retarded the great dairy industry of Canada. Our exports of condensed milk and milk powder have declined from 41,249,500 pounds in 1926 to 31,982,300-a decrease of almost 10,000,000 pounds. Worst of all, however, these declines are associated with and dependent upon a decrease in the source of supply, the milch cows, to an extent of over
100.000.	Surely no further proof is necessary to show that so far as Canada is concerned the dairy industry is in an unhealthy condition.
Coming next to beef, we find in the matter of export a decline of 25,000,000 pounds in 1929 as compared with 1927; a decline of
16.000.	000 pounds as compared with 1928, and
at the same time an increase in our imports of 5,000,000 pounds in 1929 over 1927 and
2,250,000	pounds over 1928.
In the matter of pork exports, we find also very large declines in 1929 as compared with the years 1926, 1927 and 1928; we find a decline of 71,000,000 pounds in 1929 as compared with 1926, a decline of 44,000,000 pounds as compared with 1927 and a decline of
14,000,000 pounds as compared with 1928. Surely the exports of pork in these years have been on the toboggan and going down at a rapid rate. These declines are serious enough in themselves but when we find that our imports have risen to 21,000,000 pounds in 1929, an increase of 8,000,000 over 1928, we surely must be forced again to conclude that our pork industry is in a very unhealthy condition.
Taking all in all, these increases of imports and decreases of exports mean the loss to Canada, and to agriculture in particular, of many millions of dollars. It will be argued by members of the government that the home market has been consuming much more of all these products, and they will base their arguments upon the figures of production as given by the Bureau of Statistics, but again I question the accuracy of these estimated figures. The population of Canada has not increased sufficiently during the period under review to account for such great differences in the exports of these agricultural products. Are we to believe that the Canadian people have become so gluttonous that they are consuming the quantities that would be indicated by the above argument?
I for one cannot believe that we have become a nation of gluttons; I prefer to believe that the estimated figures of production are far too high, and I must conclude, Mr. Speaker, that our great basic industry, agriculture, is on the decline and in a very unhealthy condition. This conclusion apparently is shared to some extent by the Department of Agriculture, because at the present time frantic efforts are being made to bring about an increase in the production of agricultural products. At the Royal Winter Fair held in Toronto a few months ago the Minister of Agriculture urged upon the provincial ministers the necessity of bringing about an increase in all agricultural products. Basing my conclusions in so far as agriculture are concerned upon the facts elicited in the foregoing review, I again assert that our great basic industry has reached its peak and is assuming a condition of premature senile decay.
1S96
The Budget-Mr. Murphy

Just here I might refer to our National Research Council, which during the past few years has been making considerable advances. What is the use of that department continuing to pursue its researches if at the same time the government negotiates trade treaties with countries throughout the world which have a tendency to ruin and destroy these industries? That has been the case during the past three or four years.
Referring now, Mr. Speaker, to the budget presented by the Minister of Finance, we are glad to note that he h&s seen fit to adjust the duty on butter, and that he intends to negotiate a new treaty with New Zealand. He has harkened to the protestations of the dairy industry and of the opposition and has admitted that for the past four years the government, through its trade agreements, has been sacrificing the interests of the farmers, and particularly of the dairymen, upon the altar of inadequate protection. Suddenly he has been converted. Whether that conversion has been due to the protests of the Conservative party or whether it has come about because he wished to appease the wrath of the great dairying industry with a view to securing the support of those engaged in this work when the government appeals to the people, is a question which remains to be answered. At any rate the minister has been converted and, Mr. Speaker, what a conversion it has been! The annals of history will record it as comparable to that of Saul of Tarsus. What agony of mind and soul there must have been on that occasion; cold beads of perspiration must have stood forth on his brow as he heard those challenging words, Repent; repent ye, for the judgment is at hand. Truly, Mr. Speaker, it is a deathbed repentance, but one that will not deceive the thousands of farmers throughout this country who for the past four years have suffered from unfair competition for which this government alone is responsible.
I congratulate the minister on at last having seen the light, but I cannot say that my prayers will go with him on the day of judgment.
I should like to refer to the agricultural implement industry, but I have not time to deal with that question more than to make a passing reference. In the budget brought down by the minister it is provided that agricultural implements from the United Kingdom are to be on the free list. This is just one more attempt to deceive the public minid. The importation of agricultural implements from the United Kingdom during 1929 amounted to only about $142,000, while the

total importation of agricultural implements into Canada from the United States amounted to over $40,000,000. This is simply another of those very fine gestures made by the Minister of Finance in order to deceive the people of this country and particularly the farmers of the western provinces.
_ Yesterday I had the opportunity of consulting with one of the manufacturers of agricultural implements, and I asked him what effect this budget would have upon the industry in this country. He said that as far as the change in duty was concerned it would have absolutely no effect, because in the United Kingdom they do not manufacture implements which are required by the farmers of this country. I am sorry I cannot go into this matter more fully, but I just mention this one point in passing.
Now I wish to deal with the woollen industry. In going over the tariff schedules brought down by the Minister of Finance I notice, there is not one reference to any textile item, which seems rather strange after the tariff board went to the trouble of holding a hearing in this connection lasting two weeks, the proceedings of which have been printed in two very large volumes. Representatives of the different industries presented their case and, I think presented it very fairly. Just here I should like to refer to a statement made by the Minister of Finance in delivering his budget address. He said:
Might I submit that were the capacity of our productive units greater than the normal non-speculative demand for our products, there would be cause for alarm, but such is not the case.
This is the test which is submitted by the minister, and during the course of my argument I will show that this applies very forcibly to this great textile industry. Our home consumption is supplied by our Canadian production to the extent of only from 23 to 30 per cent, while the mills in this country are capable of supplying from 50 per cent to 100 per cent of our home consumption, so I think the test submitted by the minister is met fairly well. The woollen manufacturing industry was one of the earliest of the industrial occupations to be established in Canada and developed as an essential and basic form of production. It has passed through many stages of development from the small carding and fulling mills to the fully equipped manufacturing plants of to-day. By the year 1885 there were 107 complete cloth manufacturing

The Budget-Mr. Murphy
establishments in operation in, Canada, distributed among the provinces as follows:
Ontario	 76
Quebec	 18
New Brunswick	 1
Nova Scotia	 10
Prince Edward Island	 2
The industry was established in over 100 towns and villages in eastern Canada, and reached the peak of its development about 1900. It must be admitted that some of the mills were small and uneconomic producers, but on the other hand about 100 of the mills in operation at that time were equal to the average mill in England or elsewhere. The fact remains that since that date Idle industry has failed to expand and develop with the general development of Canada. As a matter of fact it has declined, the estimated drop in the production of cloth being 50 per cent, with the accompanying loss of wages and slowing up of the economic growth of Canada.
The cloth industry was sacrificed by the enactment of the British preferential tariff in 1898, and subsequent revisions. Many mills were forced to close entirely, so that in 1910 there were only 78 woollen and worsted mills in the dominion with 224 sets of cards. By 1926 there were in operation 116 plants, of which 54 manufactured cloth, 17 manufactured yarns, 17 manufactured carpets and rugs, and 28 manufactured miscellaneous woollen goods. In 1901, when the population of Canada was about 5,000,000, the Canadian mills consumed
18,100,000	pounds of raw wool; in 1926, when the population was approximately 9,000,000, they consumed 22,300,000 pounds. In 1929 there was retained in Canada 27,230,245 pounds, a considerable quantity of which is still in store. The figures of production, exports and imports of raw wool are given by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics for the years 1927, 1928 and 1929. They are as follows:

From these figures it would seem that for the past three years the number of sheep in Canada has increased with a corresponding increase in the quantity of wool produced, but the figures for the year 1920 show that the
wool clip amounted to 24,000,000 pounds valued at $5,280,000. Requests have recently been made by certain sections of the wool grow'ing industry for assistance in preserving the home market through the restoration of the duties or worsted yarns which were removed two years ago. There is a diversity of opinion as to the suitability of our home grown wools for the manufacture of fine yarns. Undoubtedly Canada can produce practically any breed of sheep, and the Department of Agriculture might serve a very useful purpose in this respect. Wool grading has been inaugurated by that department, and in 1928, 3.452,761 pounds of wool were graded. The department reports that the clip was of particularly fine quality and that it attracted the attention not only of Canadian buyers but of buyers from the United States and continental countries.
From this it would appear that Canada can produce wool of the finest quality. What must be done if this government is desirous of stimulating and supporting the sheep raising and wool industry of Canada? What is the government going to do for the farmer who raises sheep in the hope of finding a market in Canada? Is the sheep farmer to be sacrificed along with the dairy farmer upon the altar of free trade and a non-protective tariff? If the government is to assist the wool producer it is quite evident that more of the woollen goods now used arid imported into this country must be manufactured at home. It is estimated that 70,000,000 pounds of wool would be required to supply the yarns for all the woollen goods consumed in Canada, and yet, with a production of only some 20,000,000 pounds per year, the wool producer finds that his home market has been destroyed by the tariff policy of this government. The time has come-in fact it is long since past-for a revision of the tariff policy with respect to the woollen industry. More protection must be afforded if this once great and basic industry is to survive and prosper. Such a revision would aid the farmer and the sheep rancher; it would stimulate immediately the woollen manufacturing industry, and would furnish employment for thousands of male and female labourers who have been thrown out of work and forced to seek employment in the great republic to the south. It would make the machinery hum in mills which are now idle, and would restore the life blood to many small towns and cities which were once the homes of prosperous industries.
In considering the cloth industry, it is necessary to distinguish between those factories which manufacture woollen goods, such as

The Budget-Mr. Murphy

tweeds, overcoatings, blankets and yarns, from those manufacturing worsted goods. The cloth industry has suffered most from importations. In 1925 the total consumption of cloth in Canada amounted to $36,014,287, of which $11,653,477 or 32 per cent was of Canadian manufacture. In 1927 the total consumption amounted to $39,659,338, of which $11,504,654 or 28 per cent was of Canadian manufacture. These figures show that the Canadian mills supplied in 1925 only 32 per cent of the needs of the Canadian market, and in 1927, only 28 per cent. This indicates a very serious condition, especially when it is considered that these mills are capable of supplying about nineteen to twenty million dollars' worth of goods, working eight hours a day for 304 days in the year. In other words, if they supplied only one half the needs of the Canadian market their employees would have received full time employment. It will be asked why the Canadian mills were not able to supply that quantity which would give their employees full time employment. The answer is that the laid-down cost of imported cloths is somewhat less than the price at which similar goods can be produced in Canada and sold under present market conditions. This difference is due to the lower costs of production of the imported cloths, and not because our Canadian mills are not properly equipped and operated.
The difference in costs of manufacturing in Canada and the United Kingdom is made up as follows:
1.	Difference of rates of wages in direct labour, indirect labour and fixed charges; the latter due to: (a) lower wages paid in manufacturing mill supplies, doing mill and machinery repairs, erecting mill buildings and operating rail transport; (b) better construction of buildings in Canada to stand the climate-heating, et cetera; (c) duty paid in Canada on machinery and repair parts when imported, and sales tax paid on duty paid value; (d) sales tax paid in Canada on building materials.
2.	Present conditions prevent the standardization of product which prevails in England and Scotland.
The wages paid in Canada to mill employees are about two to two and a half times as much as the wages paid in the United Kingdom, and about six times as much as the wages paid in Japan. A deplorable condition exists in this great basic Canadian industry. Does the government desire to help or is it its intention to retard and ultimately destroy the woollen cloth industry? Is this industry to be forced to reduce its wage scale to that paid in the United Kingdom in order to re-

main in business? Such a reduction would be impossible in Ontario as far as female labour is concerned on account of the minimum wage laws. Surely this government does not desire to reduce the standard of living of mill employees.
In 1885 this industry had 107 mills in operation, while in 1926 there were only 41 mills still in production. Those 41 mills had a capital investment of $17,548,074; they employed 3,843 people and paid out in wages a total of $3,395,827. What is to be done? What are the mills asking for in order that they may survive? They have not asked for the abolition of the British preferential tariff, but they ask that the rates be so revised that they may obtain a more reasonable share of the Canadian trade.
At the outset I said that we must distinguish between woollen and worsted cloths. Because of the abolition of the duties on worsted yarns, the worsted cloth industry has been benefited temporarily, whereas the woollen cloth industry is left to bear the burden of increasing importations. Woollen cloth mills have not benefited by reason of the revision because of the difficulty in securing the adequate and satisfactory supply of woollen spun yarns necessary for cloth weaving purposes. There is nothing like the degree of standardization in either yarns or fabrics in the woollen cloth industry that there is in the worsted industry. In fact, it is practically impossible for a woollen cloth mill to operate successfully without its own preparatory carding and spinning equipment, which constitutes about 60 per cent of the investment in the mill.
Conditions in 1925 and 1926 were bad enough, but they are even worse to-day. Many mills have been forced to close down, while others are operating on part time with a decreased number of employees. The increased importation of low grade shoddy woollens from the United Kingdom and Europe is slowly but surely strangling the industry. If our woollen mills are to survive, something must be done to prevent these heavy importations.
Both the woollen and worsted cloth industries require yarns made from the raw product-wool. While the worsted cloth industry may temporarily benefit from the free importation of worsted yarns, it tends to destroy the demand in this country for raw wool, thereby striking a serious blow at the sheep growing industry. Surely this deserves consideration at the hands of this or any other government. As I have said before, the woollen cloth mills must manufacture their own yarns if they are to produce the various kind of woollen cloths.

The Budget-Mr. Murphy
Now let us consider what is happening in the yarn branch of the industry. The Canadian consumption of yarns in 1925 amounted to 15,812,501, of which the Canadian production was $2,500,000. In 1926 the total Canadian market for yarns was $7,043,325, of which the Canadian mills produced $3,505,077 worth. This is divided as follows:

It will be observed that Canadian mills produced only 23 per cent of the total consumption in Canada of dry spun yarns. Why is this? It is because these yarns have a duty of only one-tenth of one per cent on account of the drawback of 99 per cent.
When one considers that the estimated capacity of the Canadian mills was 80 per cent greater than their production during that period, it is readily appreciated that they were operating under very adverse conditions. Those conditions grew worse in 1927, 1928 and 1929. The importation of yarns in the last two of those years is as follows:

I therefore submit that if the wool growing branch of agriculture is to survive the small market for it, it must receive protection through yarn producing and cloth producing industries. The Canadian Woollen and Knit Goods Manufacturers' Association have asked that the drawback of 99 per cent be removed.
I would like to refer shortly to the manufacture of woollen blankets. The figures are as follows:

The bulk of Canadian production is made up of grey and fancy colour all-wool blankets. In 1927, Canadian mills manufactured about $275,000 worth, or about 33 per cent, of the Canadian consumption of white blankets, a staple commodity. The great bulk of the imports is in the staple white wool blankets. They are imported chiefly by wholesale, mail order and departmental stores and constitute the great bulk of this business at prices below 2419-1201
those which the Canadian mills can quote, in most instances below the cost of production in Canada, without any difference in quality. The grey and coloured business is comparatively small on separate lines and is very competitive between Canadian firms. Why, it may be asked, can the Canadian mills not get the white blanket business? Simply because the costs of production are higher in Canada on account of higher wages, et cetera, and therefore Canadian mills are entitled to more protection if this industry is to survive against foreign competition.
I have arguments to show that by increasing the tariff protection on these various lines we would not increase the price to the consumer. That has been the experience in Australia where the preferential duties were raised in order to protect their own industry, and in fact the price to the consumer was lower in a majority of instances. Unfortunately, however, I have not time to go into this.
Tn my constituency the woollen industry was once in a thriving condition, but owing to the tariff tinkering of the present administration some of the mills have been forced to close down, while others are working only part time. Many female and male employees have been thrown out of employment. Houses that were once the homes of contented and happy families have been deserted and are now unoccupied. This basic industry is on the decline and it will continue to decline unless the government revises its tariff policy. Therefore I appeal to the government so to revise the tariff schedules of the woollen industry that these mills may once again become the abode of a prosperous and healthy industry.
Prosperity is in the pay envelope. The pay envelope contains both demand and consumption. The wealth of a nation will depend upon the extent to which it can provide productive employment for its own people. The creation of wealth or prosperity in its broader sense is the application of labour to raw material. In Canada we possess great natural resources, the development of which is but in its infancy. To turn these into national wealth we must make use of the following classes of labour:
(a)	Men engaged in industry.
(b)	Women engaged in industry.
(c)	Men engaged in agriculture.
The whole economic and fiscal policy of the government should be directed toward the employment of as many as possible in these three groups. How can we do this in so far
The Budget-Mr. Murphy

adult. He may be courageous; be may be brave; he may be imbued with noble and lofty sentiments, but not having maturity and strength he must fail in the contest. And thus, Mr. Speaker, young Canada must fail unless assistance is provided to make the contest equal. Our growing industrial fabric requires support and assistance to overcome that inequality of conditions brought about by lower foreign standards, and that assistance can only be rendered in so far as the government is concerned in a sympathetic and protective fiscal policy. That does not necessarily mean that the tariff should be raised so high as to eliminate fair and equal competition, but it should be sufficient to counterbalance the differences that exist as a result of those lower standards. I have no fear for Canadians when they engage in a fair contest. The history of our country will furnish sufficient evidence on that count. Let us then be fair to Canada. Let us have a policy that gives Canadian workmen and Canadian industry an equal chance in this great world struggle. Let us, where there is any doubt, give Canada the benefit of the doubt and establish once and for all time that confidence so necessary for the progress and development of our country.
