subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
flatly deny the right of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), to teach a lesson in administration to whomsoever it may be, and particularly to the present government. The hon. member would have been better advised to have kept his eye on the administration of a certain company which, thanks to a memorable bankruptcy, lost thousands of dollars of the Canadian people's savings. The effects of the bankruptcy of this company, of which the hon. member was the financial sponsor, was felt as far as the county of Laval-Two Mountains. I well know that this wretched infant, dressed in all its finery and displaying its seductive charms, won over the heart of one of my constituents. I also recall that this person after having had golden dreams, awoke one morning facing the sad reality: he had lost everything. I shall not say anything further with reference to. the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, but quote to him the proverb always true: "Doctor heal thyself."
"It is a great satisfaction for any Canadian" wrote Mr. Beatty in "L'lllustration economique

et financiere" "to be able to record that Canada after 10 years of peace, has assumed a new and greatly strengthened position in the world of finance."
Indeed, we have but to glance over the budget as brought down on May 1, by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) to find out the whole truth of this statement. A decrease, within five years, of $257,800,000 in the national debt; a reduction in taxation of nearly $100,000,000 for the years 1926, 1927, 1928 and 1929, alone; a diminution of the sales tax equal to $22,000,000 in the savings of the Canadian ratepayer, for the present fiscal year; a favourable balance of $44,507,000 and a reduction of $80,000,000 in Canada's debt this year.
These sir, are the great outlines of the excellent work of this government.
Was it not Sir Thomas White, ex-Minister of Finance in a Conservative government who, a few days ago, put this country in the seventh place among the nations of the world? Was it not the same, well-informed financier who, in a generous display of sincerity, acknowledged openly his admiration for the present administration? I how wonder what Sir Thomas White will think of the speech delivered by the hon. leader of the opposition? I also wonder what will be the effect of the speech of the leader of the opposition on the ultra imperialists, and they are numerous in the party led by my hon. friend. Answering a question put by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the leader of the opposition said: "I am for the British Empire next to Canada." Will my hon. friend repeat these words, in all circumstances, at all times and everywhere in Canada?
I well recall his last touring of the province of Quebec. I also remember that the hon. leader of the opposition, during the summer of 1928, succeeded in gathering the fabulous number of 1,500 people about ten miles from Montreal, at Laprairie, in the riding of my hon. friend, the member for Laprairie Napierville (Mr. Dupuis); but I especially recall the words uttered at Waterloo by the hon. leader of the opposition, when he said: French Canadians who hear me, remember that back of your threatened liberties, back of your minority rights, rises this mighty power which we call the British Empire.
Either the leader of the opposition was sincere or he uttered what he did not wish to say. If he is sincere, it is a case of bringing out the old proverb: "How you have changed Agnel." If he was the victim of a "lapsus linguae" he should ask that corrections be made or else retract. Otherwise, I well know

The Budget-Mr. Lacombe
that the honourable members for Wellington South (Mr. Guthrie), for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and the whole advanced guard of the proud Sicambrian will exclaim: "bow down, worship what you have burned and burn what you have worshipped!"
"To me," writes the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, "it is unthinkable that Canada should ever be anything but an integral part of the British Empire.
Many years ago, the late Cecil Rhodes of South Africa, whose vision was indisputable, ran an eloquent finger across a map on which was shown Great Britain and its dominions, with South Africa at one base of the arch and Australia and New Zealand at the other, and he pointed to Canada as the keystone of that arch. That, gentleman, is a position which some Canadians, possessing more than ordinary vision, conceive to be its position in the future, a position of economic and political prominence among the nations which form the British Empire. I could not, indeed, speak eloquently of our national policy even if it were advisable to do so, however, I must confess that there is something in the picture of a strong interdependent British Empire, with its traditional standards in public life, in finance and in commerce; with its regard for justice, for law and order, that carries a certainty of increasing power and influence.
Permit me, sir, to set side by side the masterful statement of this eminent business man and financier, with the magnificent stand taken by the hon. Minister of Finance. Through his budget, he has eloquently proclaimed our proud trade position throughout the world. Can we do otherwise than keep up our excellent economic relations with the countries which are sympathetic to us? Have we any other attitude to take than to treat in a friendly way the nations which are well disposed towards Canada?
What did the Conservative government do from 1911 to 1921, in order to improve the lot of the farming class? Did it ever amend the tariff so as to protect this basic industry? No, never. It does not behoove them now to complain. We have seen them at work. The Canadian people were the victims of their squandering policy. Prolific in election promises, doctrinaire in matters of tariff; lavish, extravagant, diligent in emptying the public treasury; past masters in taunts, while remaining sycophants of the masses; demolishers of the splendid national spirit which Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government had set up; parasites trying to disparage-to their advantage-the favourable comments which have
given rise, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, the first budget of the Hon. Charles Dunning; craving for power and changing their attitude from day to day on economic questions of the utmost importance; time servers, propagandists of electioneering literature where too often the facts and truth are defaced, they desire but, one thing: live again in abundance to their hearts content, thus bringing joy to their favourites, but misfortune to the Canadian people.
The right hon. Prime Minister has just announced an appeal will be made to the people. We have known for a long time the tactics of our opponents. We are aware of the kind of struggle we shall have to face. We have no fear, knowing that the Canadian people will judge the government and its supporters, in the light of facts, healthy development and wonderful progress in trade, finance and thriftiness for which the King government is responsible. We have no fear, fully knowing that the budget of May 1, 1930, will meet the exigencies of all classes in the community. Furthermore, when our fiscal policy is dealt with and revised it will turn out to the advantage of the Canadian ratepayer.
Following up my remarks, I wish to draw the attention of the house to the tariff which deals with fruits and vegetables. On behalf of the truck gardeners of the riding of Laval-TwO Mountains, I want to warmly congratulate the Minister of Finance for having so generously responded to the just claims of our good truck gardeners. From the very outset of my career in the parliament of Canada, I drew the attention of the government on this all important problem. I put forth the complaints which reached me.
In January, 1929, I had the privilege of meeting the truck-gardeners of the province of Quebec at a congress held in Montreal. They exposed to me their needs. At the beginning of the 1929 session, I moved a resolution asking this hon. house to enact a seasonable tariff. In taking this stand, I conformed with the views of the truck-gardeners. This seasonable tariff was to be applied only during certain months of the year. On the suggestion of the late Hon. James Robb the tariff commission inquired into the claims of fruit and vegetable growers. The distinguished economists who are on this commission declared the claims of the truck-gardeners to be well founded. They gave proof of an admirable spirit of fairness. So much so that the government through its finance minister grants not only what we had requested but further gives the truck-gardeners the greatest possible assistance, fairplay and

The Budget-Mr. Lacombe
protection. A countervailing tariff on all American vegetables coming into this country; combined tariff, ad valorem and specific, on the same products. To avoid any controversy on the subject, I shall quote verbatim that part of the budget which deals with the tariff on fruits and vegetables:
In revising the customs tariff on fruits and vegetables^ the government has given serious consideration of the representations of growers and consumers, as presented on several occasions before the Tariff Advisory Board. The irregular nature of the severe competition which Canadian producers frequently face from the earlier-maturing crops of other countries has been weighed in the light of various suggested remedies, most of which were found to have inherent defects, a fact long since recognized by the growers themselves. Seasonal tariffs, for instance, are not applicable to a country such as Canada, with its extremes of distance, latitude and climate.
After careful study of the situation from all angles, we have decided to apply to fruits and vegetables a combination of specific and ad valorem duties; this combination will, it is believed, meet the urgent need of the growers during those periods when they suffer from acute instability of prices and, at the same time, guarantee to consumers, at all seasons of the year, supplies of these products at reasonable prices.
The ad valorem rate on fresh vegetables is retained at thirty per cent under the general tariff and specific minimum duties will be effective, under the general tariff, on all except green peas and green beans.
All fresh vegetables of domestic character are made free of duty under the British preferential tariff.
I am glad my hon. friends approve. In taking this action, we have had in mind the growing' ability of Bermuda and the West Indies to supply the Canadian market during the Canadian off-season, a possibility which is rendered more feasible than before, now that Canada has her own direct steamship connection with these islands, employing vessels which are specially built for efficient transportation of perishable commodities.
For electioneering purposes, our opponents already seek to incite certain associations to protest against the new tariff on fruits and vegetables. The Eastern Canada Fruits and Vegetable Jobbers Association contend that the house-keeper will have to pay for a cauliflower 40 cents instead of 25 cents, and celery will sell at 25 cents and never again at 15 cents; tomatoes at 21 cents instead of 15 cents.
Furthermore the Western Fruit Jobbers Association, also protest because, they say a tariff of 1 cent per pound will be levied on cabbages, rhubarb, cucumbers, spinach, and a tariff of 2 cents on cauliflowers, tomatoes and celery.
Let these associations be without fear! The government states the Minister of Finance, has provided for this by granting greater facili-
ties to stock the Canadian market, during the slack season, from Bermuda and the West Indies.
I am highly pleased to note that the government has remembered, as it always does, our farmers who provide us with milk, butter and cheese. Our dairy industry plays a leading part in the prosperity of the nation. Our farmers have rejoiced over the duties to be levied on butter imported from New Zealand and the bill providing for the cancellation of the treaty between Canada and that country. This sound policy will give rise to great hopes and generous emulation among the farmers of our rural districts. Through agriculture we will promote our prosperity and insure our survival as a nation. Thanks to a remarkable development of agriculture, the consumer and city worker will find on his table products grown on Canadian soil and at reasonable prices. Both the toilers of the land and city workers, in perfect harmony, will endeavour to build up a Canada constantly gaining in happiness, prosperity and greatness.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, you will, I trust, pardon my indiscretion if I state that an incomparable inspiration of patriotism has prompted the beautiful pages which you wrote on the anniversary of the fourth century of the discovery of Canada. You have been presiding for nearly ten years over the proceedings of this house. You have been occupying a seat in this parliament for the last thirty-four years. You have watched over the economic, agricultural and industrial development of our young and vast country. Our political evolution hides no secrets from you.	When a few moments ago I was
glancing over the admirable lines whose author you are, I was thinking of the immense advantages that Canada would derive from the realization of your ideals. "Memorial to the Discoverer" ("Le monument du Souvenir").	What a noble and1 generous
inspiration! To gaze on a past denoting strength and filled with heroic deeds, sailing with spread canvas in the royal wake of future, such must be the inspiration of all true Canadians.
In a masterly description which will do honour to your compatriots, the House of Commons and the " Institut de France " of which you are one of the distinguished members, you take us with you across your beloved Gaspe peninsula, the cradle of civilization and the gospel in New France. Then, foreseeing the splendour of the great manifestations and the unbounded joy of a nation deeply moved and thrilled, " already "-you say-I see the crowds moving towards the Gaspe peninsula.

The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
It is the beautiful month of July, the third or fourth day (tiers jour ou le quart) as Jacques Cartier so delightfully puts it. Automobiles form lines basking in the glorious sunshine of the coast. The bluish tinted capes stretch far out to sea; the pleasing mounts display their rounded crowns. Ships, aeroplanes gather from everywhere, swiftly splitting the rocking waves. Trains rolling in the dust from one coquettish village to another. And innumerable pilgrims, pilgrims of the memorial and pilgrims of the faith, halt over there, at Gaspe, close to the secure harbour (hable soeur) along the basin, between graceful hills. Piously, they move across the threshold of the cathedral whose cross is erected on the point (poinct), on the very spot where, four centuries ago, in the primitive forest, Jacques Cartier erected his wooden cross thirty feet high (haulte de trente-pieds) in the midst of his mariners (mariniers), the humble toilers (laboureux) of the sea, and the naive and astonished Indians.
In this beautiful literary work, you have mingled the zest of the distant past to the progress of the present. Canada, an autonomous unit in the British Empire, deems it its duty to continue under the jEgis of our new prerogatives, in peace and harmony, its ascending march towards prosperity.
Notwithstanding the despondent cries of braggers and vilifiers of their own country; notwithstanding the sharp steel of the bombastic voice of the hon. leader of the opposition! It crumbles as it strikes the granite of the present budget. We are witnessing the spectacle of a defeated army, disarmed and disabled opposition, which awaits an impending and inevitable defeat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that I was not able to follow the arguments of the previous speaker (Mr. Lacombe). That, of course, is my misfortune. But judging by the applause which greeted his remarks from that side of the house, I presume they were very much to the liking of his colleagues.
In rising to speak in this debate I do so not so much to deal with what is contained in the budget as with what is omitted from it. The activities of this government seem for some years to have been devoted to assisting almost every country in the world but Canada. Agriculture has been embarrassed by treaties which in every instance have reacted against the Canadian farmer. Manufacturing industry has been embarrassed by a continual tinkering with the tariff. This brought about uncertainty in all lines of business, for no one knew
just where the next blow would fall. Then in turn capital became alarmed; in fact it has been withdrawn in many cases, and certainly it is not available at the present time to take its part in the improvement of industry. Each year some industry has been crippled. For three or four years I have in my speeches in this house dealt with the textile business. I predicted in 1928, when the 12i per cent duty was taken off worsted yarn, that the worsted cloth business of this country would be very seriously embarrassed if not badly crippled, and it is with the object of putting the position of that industry before this house and before the people that I have risen to speak on the budget.
By the budget items, so searchingly reviewed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) this afternoon, the secondary industries in iron and steel have been seriously affected; for instance, such an industry as that making vitreous enamelware, and the washing machine industry. In the case of the industry building children's wagons and sleds, whose business is almost slaughtered by importations from the United States, the government have seen fit to reduce by an additional five per cent the tariff on these goods coming in from the United States. The difference between five per cent or seven and a half per cent, I am assured, is pretty nearly the difference in this industry between success and failure. In many cases, according to our manufacturers, toy wagons in the United States have been coming into this country undervalued. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler), has assured the house that with respect to furniture coming into this country undervalued for duty purposes, the fair market value in the country of origin will not be taken as the fair market value in Canada owing to the different conditions prevailing in the country of origin. That being the case, if he has the power which he says he has to raise the valuation for duty on furniture, I trust he will give that relief not only to furniture which is so largely manufactured in the northern portion of the county which he has the honour to represent in this house, but also to other industries which are suffering from similar unfair competition, as makers of wagons and sleds for children and many other lines.
Articles such as enamelled kitchenware, which this budget reduces from a 20 per cent to a 10 per cent British tariff, will flood this country. That is all well and good; no one wishes to bar English whiteware enamel from this country, nor do we want to bar the white-ware from any other country. However, where the importation of this product interferes with
1906	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
the product of the Canadian factories, deprives Canadian workmen of their means of livelihood and floods this country with ware that is manufactured under different conditions of labour, we have first to attend to the interests of the Canadian people. As I understand it, we are not here to legislate for any other country; we are here to look after the interests of the Canadian people. As I understand my mission in this house it is not to help pit one class of industry in this country against another; I am not here to pit the manufacturer against the agricultural worker. Our purpose must be to give every industry a fair show. Where there are such conditions as obtain in mid-European countries, and in England, where wages are very much lower than they are here, and in many midEuropean countries where the standards of living are very much lower, to my mind it is not a case where the tariff or the fiscal policy should be changed to allow the articles from these countries to enter Canada in unfair competition with Canadian made goods. Anybody who has had anything to do with employing labour knows that it is very difficult at the present time to keep this labour employed. Personally I do not understand how a great number of the labouring people are getting along. Wages are not excessively high by any means; on the contrary, they are excessively low when we consider the Canadian standard of living and the money it takes to educate a family in this country in a decent manner. So much for that part of the budget.
In the southern portion of the county of W aterloo, which I have the honour to represent in this house, we have a highly industrialised section, and one that might be regarded as almost perfectly balanced. We have an extensive rural community largely composed of prosperous farmers, and ninety-five per cent of the produce of the farms in that county and in the surrounding counties is consumed in the counties themselves. To my mind that is an ideal situation and one which the Minister of Finance might well have kept in mind when he was framing his budget; the ideal situation would seem to be where there is, as nearly as possible, a balanced community of consumers and producers.
I wish to say a word or two about the dairying industry. A much belated attempt has been made in this budget to right a very grievous wrong done to this industry, which has been very largely destroyed by the huge importations of butter from New Zealand. If this budget is not too late in its attempt 
to revive the dairying industry I trust that dairying will be put back on a proper foundation. I have many letters from farmers in South Waterloo complaining about the very unfair competition of New Zealand butter making what was a very lucrative part of their business only a shadow of its former self. Perhaps I might illustrate the condition of the dairying industry in that section of the country by giving to the house the prices of churning cream, which controls the price of butter. I shall give the price per pound of No. 1 churning cream for the first four months of 1930 as compared with the first four months of 1929:

During tne last three or four years I have on several occasions referred to the textile industry, and more particularly that part of the industry relating to woollens and worsted cloths. In the constituency from which I come there are two very large industries of this nature and several smaller ones. One of the large industries which formerly employed between 800 and 900 people is now employing four or five hundred people, who are working only on short time. I may say this is almost entirely due to the fact that in 1928, this government took off the 12J per cent protection on worsted yarns, and in an industry of this kind, where wool was washed, combed, carded and spun into yarn, with the heavy work being done by the heads of families and the work at the looms more or less handled by female help, one can understand the serious situation which was created in

The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
towns with a population of from 2,500 to
3,000.	That is only one instance. In another factory in another town, where 270 people were employed in making woollen cloths, as distinguished from the worsted mill, since last November they have been working four days a week, and they do not know just where they are heading at the present time. Certainly they are losing a great deal of money. Hon. gentlemen can readily understand that in small towns where they have one or two of these industries this is a very serious matter, and if any words of mine are taken by the government to indicate the gravity of the situation. I shall be well content.
The condition of the woollen industry in Canada continues to be such as to give the greatest concern to those who have a sincere interest in the future of this industry. The attempts made by the present government during recent years cannot be described as other than futile and complete failures instead of being helpful measures for this important industry, as no doubt they were intended to be. Undoubtedly Canada has vast potentialities for greater and more comprehensive development in every line of industry and this woollen industry, which is fundamentally next to the great agricultural industry, is very important to the country at large. Now the situation is that one of the most flourishing of our great industries for years has been almost hopelessly struggling to avoid being completely submerged by the unfair competition to which it has been exposed. The importance of this industry was vividly impressed upon the people of this country during the stress of the war period, when the need for native sources of supply to meet the actual clothing requirements of our civil as well as our military population was emphatically brought home to all who were old enough to be impressed with this matter.
On former occasions I have alluded to the inadequacy of the attempts which have been made by the government to enable this branch of Canadian industry to make progress. It is clear to me, as it is clear to others who are located in communities where woollen and worsted manufacturing plants have been struggling bo continue in operation against great odds, that the warnings issued by those who were qualified to know what would be the effect of various changes introduced by the government did not receive from the government and its advisers the consideration which they deserved. From any action which has been taken by the government, these warnings from qualified, sincere and responsible men, to which it was frequently compelled to listen,
might as well have been the cries of immature and irresponsible children. No constructive action has been taken by the government up to this moment; such palliative measures as have been introduced have turned out to be anything but constructive in the final analysis. As a matter of fact they have been destructive to the well-being of the industry and to the welfare of the many citizens of this country who had a right to look to this industry for their livelihood.
Just here I should like to refer to the meetings which were held between the representatives of the textile industry and the tariff board. These representatives appeared on several occasions, and each time presented their case to what was thought to be a sympathetic board. In fact one prominent member of that board, to my certain knowledge, said he realized that the textile industry in this country had not been fairly treated, but no measures have been adopted looking to the relief of that situation.
Just what is the condition to which we have been brought by these ill-advised and badly conceived measures? If the government is cognizant of the effects of its past attitude on .the woollen and textile industry in this country, with its vast potentialities, the government must know that these warnings to .which it has listened from time to time were worthy of greater attention than they received. I have absolute knowledge of the situation in my own constituency as well as in other parts of the country, and I know I am not misstating the facts when I say that to-day there is not a single wool combing plant in operation in Canada. Wool combing machinery which was installed in various worsted mills at a cost of millions of dollars and which, in the .past, combed millions of pounds of wool from Canada and other parts of the British Empire, at present is not being worked to 5 per cent of its capacity, and the numerous employees of these combing plants have been obliged to seek employment in other lines of industry which, as everyone knows, is not easily found with conditions as they exist to-day. Visit any of the combing plants in Hespeler, in Sherbrooke, in Campbellford, in Guelph or at any other point, not to mention that other large plant in Trenton which within the past year or two has been completely dismantled, with the machinery shipped to the United States; seek confirmation of this statement, if you will, and you will find the fact to be as I have stated. There is not one of these plants at present consuming five per cent of the wool which it
1908	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Waterloo)
could consume if this industry received proper consideration from the government. They are all practically closed down.
Not only has the wool combing industry of this country been given the quietus, but the worsted spinning plants of the whole Dominion are rapidly going into the discard and millions of dollars invested capital are being rendered unproductive. Hundreds of the employees of these spinning mills are only working a few days a week if, indeed, they are fortunate enough to have any employment at all in this industry for which they have been trained. I feel absolutely warranted in stating that the spinning equipment for woollen worsted yarns in Canada is not being employed at present to one half its normal day work capacity, and now I am speaking only of those mills which are fortunate enough to be working at all. A number of these well equipped spinning mills with the latest machinery are completely closed down, with not a wheel turning. The Orillia worsted spinning mill, with its 5,000 spindles, is a case in point. The worsted spinning plant at Milton is also completely closed, and scores of people in these places have left the industry altogether; 110 or 115 hands in Orillia have been forced out of employment. With all the spinning plants in the Ontario mills thus suffering from want of work, we have the same reports from the industry in British Columbia and in the eastern provinces.
Hon. members should bear in mind that this condition has not been brought about because we have an over-supply of such factories or equipment in Canada. We have not enough spinning machinery in Canada to take care of our normal requirements. The fact is that while our present mills are standing idle the importation of woollen yarns, already spun abroad in mills where the wages paid are much lower than those in Canada, is continuing to the extent of millions of pounds

I do not think that anyone will argue that wages in Canada are too high. Surely $13, $15 and $17 per week are not living wages. When our workers are forced into competition with labour at $5, $6 and $7 per week, how can they possibly maintain a decent standard of living and raise a family? It simply cannot be done. These facts which have been put before the government year after year, not only from this side of the house but by the Tariff Advisory Board, should have been given more consideration than apparently they have received. Thirty odd years ago there were in this country many cloth factories making just such fabrics as in the manufacture of which Canadian wool can be most advantageously used, fabrics of a kind specially favoured by farmers and others who desire first and foremost good wearing qualities in their apparel. But on account of insufficient tariff protection and in particular the inequitable manner in which the British preference has been found, by experience, to operate, large numbers of these mills have been forced to the wall. In spite of the unquestionable worth and durability of their products, they have been unable to hold their own in the domestic market, the market of the country to which they were indigenous; against the veritable flood of importations with which they have toad to contend. As a result, Canadian wool that a few years ago sold at from seventeen to twenty-five cents per pound is to-day being offered by the farmers in my constituency at eight cents per pound, with no buyers. Everything is favourable for its enlargement with a country consuming more wool per capita than any other country in the world and with climatic and other conditions made to order. I hope I have put the case of the woollen and textile people before the house in an intelligent manner. I have tried to do so to the best of my ability. It is not fair to select any two or three or four industries and cripple them as the government is doing to-day. Huge sums of money are invested in these industries. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on this the occasion of his first budget. I recall the time twenty-one years ago when I had the honour of presiding as chairman at a meeting addressed by the present Minister of Finance and I remember that at that time he struck me forcibly as being no ordinary man. I expressed my opinion later to the audience that he was a man well worth -while keeping in one's eye and that he would make his mark. I am glad to see that he has fulfilled my prediction. At that time the minister did not have the air of self-confidence that he has to-day. He was then a very young farmer who was active in voicing the wrongs of his class and in putting forward suggestions for a remedy. Needless to say, sir, the remedies that he suggested at that time are not in the budget that is before us to-day.
There are many provisions in this budget that are satisfactory to me and will be satisfactory to my constituents. There are very many that are unsatisfactory. One of the unfortunate things about these budgets is that no matter whether a member votes for or against the budget he always finds himself voting against some things that he wants and for some things that he does not want. However, we must take the budget items in the aggregate and vote either for or against the budget.
In making a general analysis of the budget, I find that there are 270 items announced by the Minister of Finance as having the duty lowered. These are articles mostly imported from Great Britain. Of that number I find that 96 items apply exclusively to manufacturing. I am not complaining of the fact that reductions are made to manufacturers, but I draw attention to that fact because I am anticipating that statements will be made throughout the country boasting of the great benefit these reductions will be to the consumer, and I think it is well to point out this fact because with respect to these particular items there are no provisions for extending the benefit of the reduction to the consumer.
Of the other items there are at least 100 in respect to which there are no imports, and therefore for all practical purposes they can be wiped off the list of reductions. Among them are wheat, barley, buckwheat, tallow, hay and straw, live hogs, beeswax, eggs, oatmeal, cornmeal, potatoes, sugar beets, cider and sewing machines. These articles, previously dutiable, are now put on the free list when imported from Great Britain. But there are no importations of these goods and likely never will be, and the list of reductions is reduced accordingly.
A great many of the fruit items that are put on the free list when imported from the British Empire are fruits of a class that do not under any circumstances come in from Great Britain, the West Indies or any other part of the empire. Of the balance, I find that under ten items we imported less than $100 worth of goods under each; that under 15 other items we imported less than $1,000 under each; and that of 10 other items we imported less than $2,500 under each. I do not, of course, suggest that the importations will not be greater under the reduced rates. My point is that unless there is a certain amount of trade moving in a certain channel there is very little chance of a moderate reduction of "duty forcing that trade to move in that channel. The reductions are not made upon commodities of which we import large quantities.
With respect to other items, I find that certain changes are made in the application which may nullify the reductions. Take, for instance, item 409e-spraying and dusting machines, and so forth. There is a new phrase inserted in that item, "for farm purposes only." That phrase was not in the old item. The same phrase is included in item 409f- hay loaders, hay tedders, potato planters, potato diggers, and so forth. Both these items were previously dutiable under the British preference and are now put on the free list, but there is a possibility that with the addition of this phrase "for farm purposes only" they may be deprived of the benefit of being put on the free list.
May I refer to item 448 in the old tariff, under which a certain class of farm machinery had the duty raised from 10 to 30 per cent by the application of a provision of that kind? This item covers a certain class of farm implements for farm purposes. Some time ago the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) instructed, I understand, the collectors that in order for these

Further on he said:
As a great exporting nation our course must be the contrary one of facilitating trade with those who facilitate trade with us.
It seems to me that if the minister had taken his own words seriously the first thing he would have done would be to do away with or modify this 50 per cent regulation. This regulation was introduced in the 1928 budget. The Minister of Finance at that time announced that the object was to foster inter-imperial trade. Well, I am objecting to this just as much on moral grounds as economic grounds. If there had been a reason for giving our manufacturers increased protection, then the government should have come out in the open and said so and not have resorted to this subterfuge. That is one of the objections I have. At the time it was pointed out to the then Minister of Finance by members from these benches that the effect would be to increase the tariff, not to reduce it. On one occasion the present Minister of Finance gave us an assurance- and he said he was speaking on the authority of the then Minister of Finance-that the regulation would not be allowed to have that effect. Later the Prime Minister definitely

The Budget

Mr. Campbell
export of Lancashire textiles is made unusually difficult by Canadian tariff barriers? We shall welcome shipload after shipload of Canadian wheat at Liverpool, or any other English port, so long as we know that those ships will load up with English products-coal, steel, machinery, textiles, hosiery, glass and china ware, and so on-for the return trip to Canada.
Mr. Thomas must take a firm stand here. He need have no fears on the matter, for the whole nation is solid on the subject. His job is to find work and wages for the people of Great Britain. They can only secure that work and those wages if there are markets for the goods they manufacture.
During the last two or three campaigns in the prairies, Mr. Speaker, one of the principle slogans of the Liberal party has been "Don't split the low tariff vote." We have heard that on the hustings all the way from the great lakes to the Rockies; indeed I believe the slogan was coined by the present Minister of Finance, and I give him credit for originating a good political slogan, because it did have a powerful effect. I think that slogan, and the way it was presented to the people in the province of Manitoba, succeeded in destroying the Progressive organization in that province, and it did us a great deal of harm in the province of Saskatchewan. The people were told that if they organized to elect a progressive they would be splitting the low tariff vote and would let in a Tory. Some of us tried to convince them that even if they did let in a Tory they would not be any worse off as far as the tariff was concerned, because the Liberals maintained a tariff just as high as the Conservative tariff, but with newspaper propaganda and a well-organized political machine behind them, they did make that slogan very effective. It seems to me, in view of the highly protectionist features of this budget and in view of the imposition and continued enforcement of this regulation, from now on we should hear no more of the slogan "Don't split the low tariff vote."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments
will be brief. I shall confine my remarks to a few items of the budget which was brought down in the house on May 1.
First, I wish to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for having fulfilled his promise to revise the tariff.
I also wish to heartily congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) for the splendid budget he brought down last week and which will remain a memorable event in the public records of this country. I want to state that I approve entirely of this budget.
All classes in this Dominion will benefit by this budget, however, since the riding I represent is made up almost entirely of farmers, I shall especially mention the excellent results which the farmers will derive from it, and the clauses intended to protect them.
The reduction in the sales tax of 50 per cent must first be mentioned. This affects both those who make large and small purchases. This tax increases greatly the cost of living. Let us hope that in a near future the government will find it possible to abolish it completely.
The customs duty on farming implements has been reduced; that on tea is now abolished. If we consider the large consumption of tea in Canada, we can realize how important it is for the consumer to have this article on the free list.
The abolition of these duties together with the decreasing of the sales tax will have the effect of lowering considerably the cost of living.
There is, sir, a certain clause in the budget upon which I wish to especially draw the attention of the house; the one which gives Canadian farmers protection by imposing a customs duty of 4 cents per pound on butter imported from British countries, notably from Australia and New Zealand, and 14 cents for butter imported from countries which have a prohibitive tariff against us, such as the United States. The tariff on potatoes is most important. According to the present budget, should the neighbouring republic impose a duty of 90 cents per bushel on Canadian potatoes we demand the same customs duty on American potatoes, this protects us entirely against file importation of this product at all seasons. The same principle also applies to live animals. This will greatly help the farmers and will prevent the importation of animals from countries having a prohibitive tariff against our exports. Fresh and pickled meats, eggs, wheat, wheat flour, oatmeal, are many products of the farm which will equally be protected in the future. iMr. Evans.]
The products of the maple tree, which are of the utmost importance in my district, deserve also consideration by the house. It is urgent to assist as much as possible the producer of this national industry. The maple sugar industry needs new markets since the neighbouring republic, by a prohibitive tariff, has suppressed almost entirely the importations of these products. I am glad to note that a measure has been introduced by the government with a view to protecting the products of the maple tree, the measure will come into force about July 1, next. One-seventh of the total production of the maple industry in Canada comes from the county of Beauce. In 1928, Beauce produced about $580,000 worth of maple sugar and syrup. If we take into consideration the fact that this crop is collected in less than a month, we can gauge its real value to the farmer, especially when we know that this crop is collected after the winter work is done, and previous to the spring sowing, at a time when the farmer is not very busy. From 1900 to 1924, this industry was not protected and was, so to speak, at the mercy of the speculator. There was, in certain years, a great demand for this product, other years the purchases were controlled almost entirely by one buyer and the whole crop was sold at ridiculous prices. The new measure, when in force, will provide for the grading of this product and thereby prevent its imitation.
What are we to think of the abuses which have contributed to destroy almost entirely the value of this industry? What are we to think of this merchant or manufacturer who, in the capital of the province where we are at present living, bought each year four or five cars of this product in order to later on sell 25 or 30 cars of the same product adulterated.
The maple sugar producers of my district and those of the province of Quebec have formed a cooperative society, built sugar-houses and installed modern machinery, and their products are at present of a much superior quality. It is therefore absolutely necessary that this new measure be put into force without delay in order that the producer may be amply protected.
We also have, sir, in the county of Beauce another industry that needs assistance, its market is limited. I mean the industry of pulpwood as carried on by the farmer who finds it necessary to do a little lumbering of his own yearly and sell where he can find a profitable market. I see on the orders of the day a resolution, its purport is to help the paper industry in the province of Quebec and it states: that the time has come to prohibit

Calgary and Femie Railway
the exportation of pulpwood to the United States. I wish to emphatically state that I am entirely opposed to this resolution. Allow me to review the present situation and draw my own conclusions. Why are our farmers forced to export their pulpwood to the United States, when there are so many paper mills in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada? It is because Canadian companies are not desirous of purchasing pulpwood from the farmer. For the last 20 years, I have seen with my own eyes farmers obliged to pass, while drawing their wood to the railway station, through the yards of one of our principal paper mills. For twenty years, the farmers have been drawing their wood in winter and passing through the yards of this mill to reach the railway station in order to find a purchaser for their pulpwood. This state of things should not exist in Canada. The owners of paper mills should be sufficiently interested in the farmer's product to purchase at least what passes through their own yards. These same farmers must moreover pay the freight rate of $8 per cord to ship their wood to the United States. The Canadian mills could have purchased their pulpwood for a number of years past, at the rate of $10 per cord delivered. However, instead of purchasing it, they allow it to reach the American mill owners who pay $18 per cord delivered. This state of things could not exist if our Canadian mill owners had at least their future interest as well as that of Canada.
Could not the various provinces of Canada oblige our Canadian mills to take but 80 per cent of their yearly cut on the limits conceded under government licence and oblige them to purchase the other 20 per cent from the farmers, thus enabling them to sell their pulpwood on the Canadian market. Such a regulation would make it possible to absorb our own raw material and further utilize it in this country to the benefit of the whole population. If the Canadian mills were only allowed to take but 80 per cent of their yearly cut on limits under licence, they would be forced to purchase the entire cut of the farmers.
Statistics tell us that Canadian farmers cut about 1,500,000 cords of pulpwood yearly, and furthermore that the Canadian mills absorb over 7,500,000 cords yearly. We therefore know that 20 per cent out of a total of 10 to 12 million cords would more than suffice to absorb the entire output of our farmers. It would therefore be an easy matter for our Canadian mills to create a market for the farmers' needs. Thus would we prevent competition by our neighbours in the paper industry and also retain our raw material, without any disadvantage to our farmers, for should the Canadian mills find it impossible to absorb the farmers' entire output, there would still remain for the latter the foreign markets.
Briefly, I think it urgent to put into force as soon as possible the act relating to the maple sugar industry and I state that I am opposed to any resolution aiming at restricting the farmers from selling their pulpwood wherever they please.
On motion of Mr. Prevost the debate was adj owned.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe the house adjourned at 10.47 p.m.
